prompt: Summarize this scientific methods section into a single paragraph a journalist could use, explicitly flagging any part of the methodology that limits how strongly the results can be generalized: 'Participants (n=45, convenience sample from a single university) completed a 6-week intervention involving daily 10-minute mindfulness sessions via a mobile app. Self-reported stress levels were measured using the PSS-10 scale at baseline and post-intervention. No control group was used due to resource constraints; instead, a within-subjects pre-post design was employed.'

response_text: In a small-scale study examining the effects of a six-week mindfulness intervention, researchers recruited 45 participants—all students from a single university—who completed daily 10-minute mindfulness sessions via a mobile app. Stress levels were tracked using the widely used **Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10)** before and after the program, with no control group included due to budget limitations. While the **within-subjects design** (comparing each participant’s own pre- and post-measurements) strengthens the ability to detect individual changes, the study’s reliance on a **convenience sample from just one institution** and the **lack of a control group** significantly limits how broadly these results can be applied to the general population. Additionally, self-reported data may be subject to bias, and the short, app-based intervention could differ from real-world mindfulness practices.
